countries_meta.summary: Status of 15 countries on US–China economic competition as of 10 October 2026, built from news published in 2026 and WITS/UN Comtrade 2023 trade shares. The dominant 2026 pattern is that political alignment with Washington coexists with economic hedging toward Beijing. Right-wing or US-aligned governments in Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Peru all moved closer to the US on security, trade frameworks or critical-minerals MOUs. None has broken economic ties with China. Argentina renewed its full ~US$19bn PBoC swap for five years (Aug 2026) despite US calls to end it. Noboa made a state visit to Beijing (Aug 2026), praised the China–Ecuador FTA, signed cooperation documents and accepted Chinese grants, five months after signing a reciprocal trade agreement with the US. Kast met China's ambassador and plans to attend APEC in Shenzhen, while Chile is in a tariff dispute with Washington. Uruguay's Orsi signed 10+ documents in Beijing. Honduras, expected to restore ties with Taiwan, publicly denied any talks (June–July 2026). Costa Rica reaffirmed one-China. US measures in 2026 are largely tariffs and security initiatives, and they fall on allies too: the Section 301 'forced labor' tariffs from 24 July 2026 (10% on ARG, ECU, HND, MEX; 12.5% on CHL and, by inference, most others), a separate 25% Section 301 tariff on Brazil (22 July), and the decision not to renew USMCA (1 July). Hard reversals of Chinese positions are concentrated where the state controls the asset: Panama's ports, now in CK Hutchison's US$1.5bn+ treaty arbitration (20 Aug 2026), and Venezuelan oil, where the US was the main destination in Aug–Sep 2026 (Reuters data do not report a Chinese volume). Colombia's exit from the BRI is so far only a US nominee's claim (5 Aug 2026). The 2023 trade shares confirm the structural split. China is the largest export market for Chile (39.4%), Peru (36.0%) and Brazil (30.7%), and also for Panama (39.1%, probably copper-driven). The US dominates for Mexico (80.0%), Nicaragua (50.2%), Costa Rica (46.1%), Honduras (45.0%) and Colombia (28.4%). China supplies 12–34% of imports everywhere, and Paraguay's largest import source is China (33.6%) despite its Taiwan recognition. Open questions: whether Colombia formally leaves the BRI; whether Honduras switches; the outcome of the Panama arbitration and the BlackRock–MSC deal; 2024–2025 trade shares, which are not yet in WITS and show Chinese gains in Ecuador and Peru according to officials.

items.item: trade: lithium compounds to the US
items.txt: Chile (54%) and Argentina (43%) supplied 97% of US lithium imports in 2021–24, and US net import reliance for lithium exceeded 50% of apparent consumption in 2023–2025.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Lithium chapter, 'Import Sources (2021–24)' and Salient Stat)
items.q: Import Sources (2021–24): Chile, 54%; Argentina, 43%; and other, 3%.

items.item: trade: refined copper to the US
items.txt: Chile (68%), Peru (7%) and Mexico (6%) together supplied about 81% of US refined-copper imports in 2021–24 (Canada 16%). Nearly all US imports of copper ore and concentrate came from Canada. USGS put US net import reliance for refined copper at about 57% of apparent consumption in 2025.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Copper chapter, 'Import Sources (2021–24)' and Salient Stati)
items.q: Refined copper: Chile, 68%; Canada, 16%; Peru, 7%; Mexico, 6%; and other, 3%.

items.txt: Albemarle, a US-headquartered company, has operated in Chile for more than 40 years. It pumps brine at the Salar de Atacama and converts it into technical- and battery-grade lithium carbonate at its La Negra plant near Antofagasta, which also houses R&D laboratories. It employs more than 1,100 workers in Chile.
items.cite: Albemarle Corporation (2026, Chile country page)

items.txt: Freeport-McMoRan (US) owns 55.66% of Peru's Cerro Verde copper mine (Sumitomo Metal Mining 21%, Buenaventura 19.58%) and 51% of Chile's El Abra (Codelco 49%). El Abra has a solvent-extraction/electrowinning capacity of about 500 million pounds of copper cathode a year.
items.cite: Freeport-McMoRan Inc. (2026, Cerro Verde and El Abra sections)

items.txt: Serra Verde (Brazil) secured a US$565m DFC financing package that includes an option for the US government to acquire a minority equity stake. It is to be used to refinance debt and support expansion to 6,500 t of total rare-earth oxide production by end-2027 at its integrated mine-and-processing operation, which produces a mixed rare-earth carbonate.
items.cite: Mining Weekly (Creamer Media) (2026, Article body)

items.txt: ECLAC: with Mexico included, the region's exports to the US have a strongly industrial profile (autos and electronics). Excluding Mexico, they are dominated by primary products. The US took more than 80% of the region's exports of electrical machinery, and Mexico accounted for 85% of the region's high-technology manufacturing exports in 2024.
items.cite: CEPAL/ECLAC (2025, Síntesis, printed pp. 19-20 (Gráficos 3-4) and p. 24 (Gráfic)
items.q: cambia de un perfil marcadamente industrial a uno en que predominan los productos básicos

items.txt: ECLAC: in 2024 the US took more than 80% of Mexico's goods exports and almost half of the exports of Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Honduras (about 60% for the Dominican Republic), but for most South American countries the US share did not exceed 15%.
items.cite: CEPAL/ECLAC (2025, Síntesis, printed p. 18, Gráfico 3 (p. 19))
items.q: concentró más del 80% de las exportaciones totales de bienes de México

items.txt: The US direct investment position (stock) in Latin America was about US$357bn at the end of 2025 according to BEA data analysed by CREES, with Mexico 47.3%, Brazil 25.3% and Chile 10.8% of the total. CRS, also citing BEA, gives US$169.8bn for Mexico in 2025.
items.cite: Revista Mercado / CREES, citing U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (2026, Article body)

items.item: 2026 frameworks: MOUs + EXIM letters of interest
items.txt: At the February 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial, the US signed memoranda of understanding or framework agreements with Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru, among others. The financial figures cited were EXIM letters of interest (US$14.8bn for critical-minerals projects) and 'more than $30 billion in letters of interest, investments, loans and other support' over the past year (all regions), not disbursed finance.
items.cite: S&P Global Commodity Insights (2026, Article body)
items.q: memoranda of understanding or framework agreements

items.txt: US copper processing capacity is small relative to China's: in 2025 the US had 2 primary smelters, 2 primary electrolytic refineries, 14 electrowinning refineries and 4 secondary refineries. Refined output fell about 9% because of maintenance at both primary smelters, and the US exported an estimated 340,000 t of copper in ore and concentrate.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Copper chapter, 'Domestic Production and Use' and Salient St)

items.txt: The US mined an estimated 51,000 t REO of rare-earth concentrate in 2025 (Mountain Pass) but produced only about 8,900 t of rare-earth compounds and metals. Net import reliance for compounds and metals rose to 67% (from 53% in 2024), with China supplying 71% of these imports in 2021–24, while the US was a net exporter of concentrates.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Rare Earths chapter, 'Domestic Production and Use', Salient )

items.txt: US lithium production comes from a single continental brine operation in Nevada (Albemarle's Silver Peak, which the company calls the only active lithium resource in the US), and two companies make downstream lithium compounds from domestic or imported feedstock. Production data are withheld. USGS lists US reserves of 4.4 Mt.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Lithium chapter, 'Domestic Production and Use')

items.item: US share of refining by geography vs ownership
items.txt: IEA: the US holds about 1% of refined copper and lithium production by geography, but US companies own over 10% of refined copper production and almost 15% of lithium chemical production worldwide. Their assets abroad include Albemarle's lithium carbonate plant in Chile (see X-S230).
items.cite: International Energy Agency (2025, Chapter 1, section 'Price declines for critical minerals are)

items.item: Natural graphite production, reserves and US import reliance
items.txt: USGS MCS 2026 natural graphite: China mined an estimated 1.4 Mt in 2025 and Brazil 65,000 t (world 1.8 Mt). Reserves were 100 Mt in China and 74 Mt in Brazil (world 310 Mt). The US produced no natural graphite and was 100% import-reliant, with China supplying 46% and Mexico 12% of US imports in 2021–24.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Graphite chapter, 'World Mine Production and Reserves'; 'Dom)

items.txt: IEA: China is the dominant refiner for 19 of the 20 energy-related strategic minerals analysed, with an average market share of around 70%. The average market share of the top three refiners of key energy minerals rose to 86% in 2024 from about 82% in 2020.
items.cite: International Energy Agency (2025, Executive summary, printed p. 8; IEA news release of 21 May )

items.item: Refined copper production and refinery-to-mine ratio
items.txt: USGS MCS 2026 refined copper: estimated 2025 refinery production was 14.0 Mt in China, 1.7 Mt in Chile, 0.85 Mt in the US, 0.48 Mt in Mexico and 0.34 Mt in Peru (world 29 Mt). China refines about eight times its own mine output, while Chile refines about a third and Peru about an eighth of what they mine.
items.cite: U.S. Geological Survey (2026, Copper chapter, table 'World Mine and Refinery Production an)

items.txt: Endowments and capabilities are distributed differently. The LAC countries examined hold large shares of world copper reserves (Chile 18%, Peru 9%, Mexico 5%), lithium reserves (Chile, Argentina and Brazil about 38%, plus Bolivia's 23 Mt of resources), and rare-earth and graphite reserves (Brazil second to China in both). But on every capability indicator collected they sit well below both the US and China: R&D at or below 1.2% of GDP, under 1,350 researchers per million, and logistics scores of 3.2 or less.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S202; X-S203; X-S205; X-S207; X-S216; X-S217; X-S222

items.txt: The 'US innovates, China manufactures' dichotomy is not supported. China's manufacturing value added (US$4.82tn, 24.7% of GDP in 2025) far exceeds the US level (US$2.50tn, 10.5% of GDP in 2021). But China also spends 2.58% of GDP on R&D, files about six times as many resident patent applications as the US, and exports more high-tech goods (US$857bn vs US$233bn; similar shares of 26% and 24%). The US remains ahead in R&D intensity (3.45%) and researcher density (4,937 vs 2,107 per million). The two overlap in high-technology production, not just in demand for LAC inputs.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S216; X-S217; X-S218; X-S219; X-S220; X-S221

items.txt: LAC complements China mainly at the upstream stage. China mines only about 8% of world copper but refines about 48%, and it is the dominant refiner of 19 of 20 key minerals. Meanwhile, six raw or lightly processed commodities make up 72% of LAC exports to China, and China buys about a third of LAC mining exports. China's processing capacity therefore absorbs exactly the ores and concentrates that LAC (which refines only about a fifth of what it mines, excluding lithium) does not process at home.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S203; X-S204; X-S213; X-S215; X-S225; X-S228

items.txt: LAC complements the US differently: as a supplier of processed minerals and as a manufacturing partner. Chile and Argentina supplied 97% of US lithium imports (as compounds), and Chile, Peru and Mexico supplied about 81% of US refined-copper imports. Mexico, which sends more than 80% of its exports to the US and accounts for 85% of LAC high-tech manufacturing exports, is integrated into US value chains (autos and electronics). The US relationship with LAC is thus weighted towards midstream products and manufactures, and towards Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S208; X-S209; X-S220; X-S226; X-S227

items.txt: The geography is divided. Mexico, Central America and the Dominican Republic send roughly half to more than 80% of their exports to the US. For most South American countries the US share is at most 15%, China is the first trading partner of South America, and 93% of LAC exports to China come from South America. US–China rivalry therefore plays out on different terrain in the two subregions: market dependence on the US in the north, commodity demand from China in the south.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S223; X-S224; X-S225; X-S227

items.txt: The US and China overlap, and partly compete with LAC, as mineral producers, not only as buyers. The US mines about 1.0 Mt of copper, 38 Mt of iron ore and 51,000 t REO of rare earths, and holds lithium reserves (4.4 Mt) equal to Argentina's. China mines more lithium than Chile in 2025 (62,000 vs 56,000 t) and 69% of the world's rare earths. Both also own LAC assets: US firms own about 15% of world lithium-chemical output (e.g. Albemarle in Chile) and run Freeport's Cerro Verde and El Abra, alongside Chinese-owned mines (Las Bambas, Toromocho) and stakes (Tianqi in SQM).
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S201; X-S202; X-S203; X-S205; X-S206; X-S214; X-S230; X-S231

items.txt: The US's binding constraint in LAC minerals is midstream processing capacity, which is where China is strongest. The US has 2 primary copper smelters, about 1% of world rare-earth refining, imports 71% of its rare-earth compounds and metals from China, and has no natural graphite production. US policy instruments in 2025–26 were mostly frameworks, MOUs and non-binding EXIM letters of interest. The main financed LAC case found is DFC's US$565m package for Serra Verde in Brazil. The US can offer finance, a market for refined products and diplomatic frameworks, but it cannot yet absorb LAC ores and concentrates at scale as China does.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S207; X-S210; X-S211; X-S213; X-S232; X-S233

items.txt: The US remains LAC's largest economic partner by trade (44% of exports, 28% of imports in 2024) and by recorded FDI stock (about US$357bn, almost half in Mexico). China's 13% and 22% trade shares and its under-recorded FDI are smaller in aggregate but concentrated in South American minerals, energy and food. So the claim that China 'continues to expand' refers to specific sectors and subregions where its processing and demand capabilities match LAC endowments, not to an overall displacement of the US.
items.cite: Synthesis of X-S223; X-S224; X-S225; X-S229; X-S228

us.summary: Adding the US shows that endowments and capabilities do not line up as 'LAC = resources, US = innovation, China = manufacturing'. On endowments (USGS MCS 2026), LAC holds large shares of world copper reserves (Chile 18%, Peru 9%, Mexico 5%), lithium reserves (Chile, Argentina and Brazil about 38%, plus Bolivia's 23 Mt of resources, not reserves) and rare-earth and graphite reserves (Brazil second to China). The US and China are also substantial miners: the US mines 1.0 Mt of copper and 51 kt of rare earths and has lithium reserves equal to Argentina's, and China out-mined Chile in lithium in 2025. On capabilities (WDI), both powers overlap: China leads in manufacturing value added, patents and high-tech export value, while the US leads in R&D intensity and researcher density. Their high-tech export shares are similar (26% vs 24%). Every LAC country sits far below both. The decisive difference is midstream. China refines about 48% of world copper from 8% of mine output and is the dominant refiner for 19 of 20 key minerals (IEA). The US has 2 primary copper smelters, about 1% of rare-earth refining and 100% import reliance for graphite, though US firms own about 15% of world lithium-chemical output (e.g. Albemarle in Chile). LAC refines only about a fifth of what it mines (excluding lithium). So LAC complements China upstream: six commodities make up 72% of LAC exports to China, and China buys about a third of LAC mining exports. LAC complements the US as a supplier of processed minerals (Chile and Argentina supply 97% of US lithium imports; Chile, Peru and Mexico about 81% of refined copper imports) and as a manufacturing partner (Mexico). Why this matters for the central question: the US is still LAC's largest trade partner (44% of exports) and investor (about US$357bn of FDI stock, provisional), but its links concentrate in Mexico and Central America. China's demand and processing capacity fit South America's endowments in a way US policy instruments do not yet replicate. Those instruments are mostly MOUs and letters of interest; DFC's US$565m for Serra Verde is the main financed case. This structural fit, rather than discourse, helps explain China's sectoral consolidation. Counter-evidence and open questions: the US share of LAC trade still far exceeds China's; Chile and Argentina do process lithium locally; and Chinese FDI is under-recorded, which makes FDI comparisons unreliable.
gaps: IEA country-level refining shares for lithium chemicals (e.g. Chile, Argentina), copper and rare earths could not be extracted: values appear only in charts (GCMO 2025 pp. 26-29; GCMO 2026 p. 31). Only China's aggregate shares, the US geography/ownership shares and LAC regional figures were verified.

BEA country-level US direct investment position tables (apps.bea.gov xlsx/iTable) were blocked to the research tool; LAC total and BRA/CHL shares rely on a secondary analysis (CREES via Revista Mercado), marked provisional. Only Mexico (US$169.8bn, CRS citing BEA) is double-sourced. No BEA mining-industry breakdown for LAC was obtained.

Chinese FDI stock in LAC from MOFCOM's Statistical Bulletin (dominated by Cayman Islands and British Virgin Islands) and from the China Global Investment Tracker was not retrieved; the stream relies on existing records X-S025 and X-S028 for the Chinese side.
WDI has no US manufacturing value added after 2021 and no Peru researcher data; Brazil's researcher figure dates from 2014.
Electricity generation by country was not collected (optional in the task).

USGS figures were read through a PDF text extractor that merges superscript footnote numbers with values. Ambiguous cells (iron-ore reserves, Mexico graphite production) were omitted, and interpreted cells (Chile and Argentina lithium 2024, US rare earths 2024) are flagged in their limitations.

Primary text of the February 2026 critical-minerals frameworks (State Department) and of the DFC Serra Verde commitment was not found; S&P Global and Mining Weekly were used. Disbursement status of Serra Verde funds is unknown.
No verified evidence was found of Minerals Security Partnership projects financed in LAC, or of EXIM loans actually disbursed to LAC mineral projects.

X-C201.limitations: Reserve shares are my calculations from USGS tables. Capability indicators use different years (Brazil researchers 2014). LAC is heterogeneous: Brazil (R&D 1.19%) and Argentina (1,313 researchers per million) are well ahead of Bolivia (0.06%, 63).

X-C202.claim: The 'US innovates, China manufactures' dichotomy is not supported. China's manufacturing value added (US$4.82tn, 24.7% of GDP in 2025) far exceeds the US level (US$2.50tn, 10.5% of GDP in 2021). But China also spends 2.58% of GDP on R&D, files about six times as many resident patent applications as the US, and exports more high-tech goods (US$857bn vs US$233bn; similar shares of 26% and 24%). The US remains ahead in R&D intensity (3.45%) and researcher density (4,937 vs 2,107 per million). The two overlap in high-technology production, not just in demand for LAC inputs.
X-C202.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S216, X-S217, X-S218, X-S219, X-S220, X-S221
X-C202.limitations: Patent counts are not quality-adjusted. US manufacturing data in WDI stop in 2021. High-tech export classifications count assembly as well as design.

X-C203.claim: LAC complements China mainly at the upstream stage. China mines only about 8% of world copper but refines about 48%, and it is the dominant refiner of 19 of 20 key minerals. Meanwhile, six raw or lightly processed commodities make up 72% of LAC exports to China, and China buys about a third of LAC mining exports. China's processing capacity therefore absorbs exactly the ores and concentrates that LAC (which refines only about a fifth of what it mines, excluding lithium) does not process at home.
X-C203.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S203, X-S204, X-S213, X-S215, X-S225, X-S228
X-C203.limitations: This is a structural fit, not a statement about intent. Chilean cathodes and lithium carbonate are processed products, so 'upstream only' overstates the pattern for Chile.

X-C204.claim: LAC complements the US differently: as a supplier of processed minerals and as a manufacturing partner. Chile and Argentina supplied 97% of US lithium imports (as compounds), and Chile, Peru and Mexico supplied about 81% of US refined-copper imports. Mexico, which sends more than 80% of its exports to the US and accounts for 85% of LAC high-tech manufacturing exports, is integrated into US value chains (autos and electronics). The US relationship with LAC is thus weighted towards midstream products and manufactures, and towards Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.
X-C204.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S208, X-S209, X-S220, X-S226, X-S227
X-C204.limitations: US import-source shares cover 2021–24 and are shares of US imports, not of LAC exports. Excluding Mexico, LAC exports to the US are mainly primary products (ECLAC), so the contrast with China is sharpest for Mexico and Central America.

X-C205.claim: The geography is divided. Mexico, Central America and the Dominican Republic send roughly half to more than 80% of their exports to the US. For most South American countries the US share is at most 15%, China is the first trading partner of South America, and 93% of LAC exports to China come from South America. US–China rivalry therefore plays out on different terrain in the two subregions: market dependence on the US in the north, commodity demand from China in the south.
X-C205.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S223, X-S224, X-S225, X-S227
X-C205.limitations: Based on regional aggregates and ECLAC text; Colombia and Ecuador send larger shares to the US than most of South America.

X-C206.claim: The US and China overlap, and partly compete with LAC, as mineral producers, not only as buyers. The US mines about 1.0 Mt of copper, 38 Mt of iron ore and 51,000 t REO of rare earths, and holds lithium reserves (4.4 Mt) equal to Argentina's. China mines more lithium than Chile in 2025 (62,000 vs 56,000 t) and 69% of the world's rare earths. Both also own LAC assets: US firms own about 15% of world lithium-chemical output (e.g. Albemarle in Chile) and run Freeport's Cerro Verde and El Abra, alongside Chinese-owned mines (Las Bambas, Toromocho) and stakes (Tianqi in SQM).
X-C206.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S201, X-S202, X-S203, X-S205, X-S206, X-S214, X-S230, X-S231
X-C206.limitations: Ownership comparisons are illustrative; this stream did not compile a full ownership census of LAC mines. Chinese asset examples are existing events X-E607, X-E609 and X-E617.

X-C207.claim: The US's binding constraint in LAC minerals is midstream processing capacity, which is where China is strongest. The US has 2 primary copper smelters, about 1% of world rare-earth refining, imports 71% of its rare-earth compounds and metals from China, and has no natural graphite production. US policy instruments in 2025–26 were mostly frameworks, MOUs and non-binding EXIM letters of interest. The main financed LAC case found is DFC's US$565m package for Serra Verde in Brazil. The US can offer finance, a market for refined products and diplomatic frameworks, but it cannot yet absorb LAC ores and concentrates at scale as China does.
X-C207.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S207, X-S210, X-S211, X-S213, X-S232, X-S233
X-C207.limitations: Policy implementation may lag; projects announced in 2026 may reach financial close later. EXIM's Argentina framework (existing X-E673) is single-source and not yet disbursed.

X-C208.claim: The US remains LAC's largest economic partner by trade (44% of exports, 28% of imports in 2024) and by recorded FDI stock (about US$357bn, almost half in Mexico). China's 13% and 22% trade shares and its under-recorded FDI are smaller in aggregate but concentrated in South American minerals, energy and food. So the claim that China 'continues to expand' refers to specific sectors and subregions where its processing and demand capabilities match LAC endowments, not to an overall displacement of the US.
X-C208.source_title: Synthesis of records X-S223, X-S224, X-S225, X-S229, X-S228
X-C208.limitations: FDI figures are not comparable (BEA position vs ECLAC inflows by immediate origin vs commercial databases); the US FDI country values are provisional. The US share of LAC trade fell substantially since 2000.

X-S301.claim: A Federal Reserve Board decomposition attributes about 53% of the growth in Mexican exports to the US between 2014-17 and 2021-24 to trade diversion from the 2018-19 US tariffs on China. About 14% reflects Chinese production or processing in Mexico, about 38% diversion through non-Chinese firms, and less than 1 percentage point direct transshipment from China.

X-S301.author_institution: Maria Aristizabal-Ramirez, Chris A. Avalos, Emma Rosenbaum, Eva Van Leemput; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
X-S301.locator: Figures 3 and 4 and the accompanying text; the accessible-data version gives the bar values (trade diversion about US$65bn of about US$125bn annualised growth; Chinese production in Mexico about US$17bn; transshipment about US$1bn)
X-S301.limitations: The authors have no firm-ownership data and identify the Chinese 'backdoor' from trade flows, so the estimates are 'informative bounds'. Transshipment is defined strictly: US imports from China fall while Mexican imports from China and exports to the US both rise, Chinese exports to Mexico outpace exports elsewhere, and Mexican export growth does not significantly exceed import growth from China. Covers only goods tariffed in 2018-19.
X-S301.quote: direct transshipment from China is negligible, accounting for less than 1 percentage point
X-S301.value: trade diversion ~53%; Chinese production in Mexico ~14%; other diversion ~38%; trend ~35%; other ~12%; direct transshipment <1 pp
X-S301.indicator: Decomposition of growth in Mexican exports to the US

The stated aims are to reduce dependence on foreign inputs, protect domestic producers, raise national content of exports, integrate supply chains and correct trade imbalances.
X-E906.limitations: Galicia's note does not set out IMMEX/PROSEC treatment. Votes: Senate 76-5 with 35 abstentions; Chamber 281-24 (China Global South Project, 11 Dec 2025). Affected countries per Clark Hill include China, Korea, India, Indonesia, Russia, Thailand and Turkey.
X-E906.quote: incrementar el contenido nacional de los productos exportados

X-E907.claim: A second tariff decree (DOF, 23 April 2026, evening edition) modifies import duties on 185 tariff lines (5-35%) and amends the PROSEC sectoral promotion decree, setting specified flat-rolled and alloy steel lines to duty-free for the electrical, electronics and automotive programmes. It takes effect 24 April 2026.
X-E907.source_title: Segunda reforma arancelaria: el impacto de la reducción en PROSEC
X-E907.locator: Article body (art. 5, fracc. I, II b and XIX of the PROSEC decree)
X-E907.limitations: The DOF text was not opened. The article title speaks of a 'reduction' in PROSEC, but the summary we obtained describes lines being set to 'Exento'; the exact direction of change for each programme needs checking against the DOF. No official rationale was stated.

X-E908.claim: At the USMCA six-year joint review on 1 July 2026, the United States declines to confirm a 16-year extension. Mexico and Canada support renewal. The agreement stays in force to 2036, subject to annual joint reviews under Article 34.7.
X-E908.source_title: Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on USMCA Joint Review
X-E908.author_institution: Office of the United States Trade Representative
X-E908.limitations: The USTR statement does not mention China, rules of origin or transshipment. White & Case and CRS report that bilateral US-Mexico rounds cover automotive rules of origin, steel and aluminium, and economic security.
X-E908.quote: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form.

X-E909.claim: A 10% Section 301 tariff on imports from Mexico takes effect after USTR finds that Mexico does not effectively enforce its ban on imports made with forced labour. USMCA-compliant goods and products under Section 232 are exempt.
X-E909.limitations: A parallel Section 301 investigation into excess industrial capacity was still ongoing (CRS, Aug 2026). Given 88% USMCA compliance (X-S311), the direct coverage is limited.
X-E909.quote: imposed a 10% tariff on imports from Mexico, effective July 24, 2026

X-E910.claim: The White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy publishes 'The Great Transshipment Scam', listing more than 40 economies as risk routes for China-linked goods and placing Mexico in Tier 1 ('Diversified Scale Leaders'). It cites existing EAPA authority and a CBP AI tool in development ('Detective Border'). It gives no Mexico-specific estimate.
X-E910.source_title: White House Transshipment Report Signals Increased Scrutiny
X-E910.limitations: We did not open the report itself. Its global figures (for example US$75bn/yr transshipment; US$34.2-303bn potentially affected trade) are model estimates with differing definitions (Latin Times, 14 Aug 2026). Per Latin Times, the report notes that Chinese parts in Mexican-assembled goods are not illegal in themselves.
participants: White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy

X-E911.claim: Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard proposes to auto suppliers, at a private meeting in Detroit, a task force with major companies operating in Mexico to reduce imports from China ahead of Trump's inauguration.
X-E911.source_title: Mexico Pitches Auto Suppliers Task Force to Curb China Imports
X-E911.limitations: The date is inferred: the article says the meeting was on the Friday before the Monday inauguration (20 Jan 2025). The page is partly paywalled.

X-E912.claim: At Canacero's 78th General Assembly, incoming president Sergio de la Maza Jiménez blames Chinese overproduction and subsidised dumping for the crisis in Mexican steel. He also criticises US Section 232 tariffs and calls for a regional North American steel policy, with Economy Secretary Ebrard present and pledging to defend domestic steel.
X-E912.source_title: Aranceles y dumping chino asestan golpe a la industria acerera
X-E912.limitations: These are statements by an interested party; only one press report was checked.
X-E912.quote: la principal razón de estas distorsiones tiene nombre y apellido

X-P301.claim: Hisense announced a US$260m appliance plant (refrigerators, dishwashers, ovens, air conditioners) in Salinas Victoria, Nuevo León, in March 2021, with about 1,000 jobs in the first stage and output intended for Mexico, the US and Canada. In March 2025 Hisense said none of its Mexican plants (Monterrey white goods; Tijuana televisions) would close and that the second stage of the Monterrey plant remained planned.
X-P301.source_title: Hisense, gigante de los electrodomésticos, abrirá una planta de manufactura en Nuevo León
X-P301.limitations: Realised investment and employment are not documented in the sources checked. Expansión (2025) describes the Monterrey-area plant as producing white goods and says about 80% of Tijuana TV output is exported. The site is understood to be in the Hofusan park, but the sources checked do not state this.

X-P302.claim: Lenovo's Monterrey 'megasite' has operated since 2014. A 180,000 sq ft second building opened in 2021 for data-centre infrastructure, producing more than 10,000 servers and 200 racks a week, and Lenovo states all its data-centre products for North American customers are made in Monterrey.
X-P302.source_title: Monterrey 'Megasite' Expands to Lead Lenovo Manufacturing in North America
X-P302.limitations: Company source; investment amount and local content not disclosed. Status after 2021 not verified in this round.
X-P302.quote: All Lenovo data center products for North America customers are manufactured in Monterrey.

X-P303.claim: Hofusan Industrial Park in Salinas Victoria, Nuevo León, a co-investment of China's Holley Group and Futong Group with Nuevo León's Santos family, announced in October 2024 plans to invest US$1bn over the coming years in about 100 additional industrial buildings.
X-P303.source_title: Hofusan Industrial Park anuncia inversión de 1,000 mdd para expandirse en Nuevo León
X-P303.limitations: No tenant list, area or realised investment in the source. The Dallas Fed notes Chinese firms were 17% of 196 new industrial-park tenants in Mexico in 2023 and about 4% of all tenants.
X-P303.quote: una coinversión entre los grupos chinos Holley Group y Futong Group

X-P304.claim: BYD's planned Mexican car plant was put on hold in July 2025. Executive vice-president Stella Li told Bloomberg the company would wait for 'more clarity', citing geopolitics. As late as November 2024 BYD executives had said the plant would go ahead, targeting the Mexican market rather than the US.
X-P304.source_title: Tesla competitor BYD axes Mexico factory plans (Business Insider via AOL)
X-P304.limitations: Characterisation differs: Business Insider's headline says 'axes' but the body describes a hold; the Dallas Fed (Sept 2025) says BYD 'canceled its planned Mexico production in July 2025'. Mexico News Daily (Nov 2024) reported BYD's earlier commitment.
X-P304.quote: We want to wait for more clarity before making our decision.
X-P304.amount_announced: not officially disclosed (~US$600m Bloomberg estimate per X-P010)

X-P305.claim: Rhodium identifies ZC Rubber's US$600m tyre investment (announced 2024) as the largest Chinese auto-parts commitment in Mexico. It estimates about US$2bn of announced Chinese auto-parts investment is at risk if US-linked automotive FDI slows, and notes CATL paused Mexican battery plans in 2022 because of US sourcing restrictions.
X-P305.source_title: A Closing Back Door? China's Evolving FDI Presence in Mexico
X-P305.limitations: Single think-tank source for ZC Rubber; company filings not checked. CATL's US$5bn figure comes from Dallas Fed (Sept 2025), which says the plans are 'on hold'.
X-P305.amount_announced: 600 million (ZC Rubber); CATL up to 5bn reported (Dallas Fed)

X-C301.claim: The simultaneous rise of Chinese imports into Mexico and of Mexican exports to the US is not sufficient evidence of circumvention. Studies that test product- and firm-level conditions find the export gains far exceed what rerouted Chinese goods could explain: the Fed puts transshipment under 1 point of growth, Banxico 0.45% of exports as an upper bound, and the Utar et al. results survive netting out Chinese imports.
X-C301.source_title: Synthesis of X-S301, X-S302, X-S314, X-S317
X-C301.limitations: All aggregate methods miss Chinese goods bought through Mexican intermediaries and product-level fraud that is small in aggregate but real (X-E903). Most studies cover the 2018-19 tariff episode; post-2025 dynamics, with much higher China tariffs, are less studied.

X-C302.claim: Unlawful transshipment and false origin declarations via Mexico are documented at the case level, as in EAPA 7801 on Chinese aluminium extrusions declared as Mexican, but no study we reviewed finds them to be macroeconomically large. US policy statements that infer transshipment from aggregate trade trends (Proclamation 10896) are assertions, not adjudicated findings.
X-C302.source_title: Synthesis of X-E903, X-S318, X-S301, X-S302
X-C302.limitations: We found no DOJ criminal case specifically involving the Mexico route in this round; the DOJ cases found (for example Repwire, Sept 2024) involved other declared origins. Mexican customs (ANAM) enforcement actions were not verified.

X-C303.claim: The China-linked channel with measurable size is production in Mexico using Chinese inputs or by Chinese-owned firms (about 14% of export growth in the Fed decomposition). The larger share of reallocation gains (about 38%) went through non-Chinese firms, notably US multinationals' Mexican subsidiaries, which also increased Chinese input purchases. This is legal under USMCA where rules of origin are met.
X-C303.locator: Fed Figure 4; Utar et al. p. 4 and Figure 9a
X-C303.limitations: The Fed attribution of the 14% to 'China' is a bound: it may overstate it if non-Chinese firms used more Chinese inputs, and understate it because non-tariffed inputs are excluded.

X-C304.claim: Estimates of Chinese content in Mexican exports are contested and depend on method and base. The Dallas Fed (citing ADB) puts Chinese value added at about 7%, while Brookings states about one-third. Value-added sources agree that domestic value added is roughly half (48-51%), US content about 17-19%, and that Mexican value added in electronics rose after 2018. 'Chinese content rising' and 'Mexican value added rising' can both be true.
X-C304.limitations: TiVA-type data lag (latest years 2018-2022) and do not capture post-2023 reorganisation. Normative USMCA regional value content and analytical value added are different concepts (Banxico note 2).

X-C305.claim: Chinese FDI in Mexico is growing but small relative to US FDI: officially about 1% of inflows and on private estimates about 10-13% of the US stock. Announcements greatly exceed realisations. The most-scrutinised projects (BYD, CATL, Ganfeng) have not materialised, which suggests Chinese manufacturing in Mexico depends on US-market access conditions and on Chinese and Mexican government approvals.
X-C305.source_title: Synthesis of X-S307 to X-S310, X-S315, X-P304, X-P305
X-C305.limitations: The true size of Chinese FDI is unknown because of routing through Hong Kong and other jurisdictions. H1 2026 official data showing a record US$596m (X-S315) are preliminary.

X-C306.claim: The main empirical studies converge on reallocation and trade diversion with continued indirect dependence on China, not on decoupling or large-scale fraud. Freund et al. find countries replacing China are embedded in Chinese supply chains and see faster import growth from China, with nearshoring confined to border countries. Alfaro and Chor describe a 'great reallocation' with higher unit costs from Mexico. Utar et al. find GVC relocation to Mexico.
X-C306.locator: Freund et al. abstract and p. 15; Alfaro and Chor pp. 5, 30, 33; Utar et al. abstract
X-C306.limitations: Freund et al. do not test transshipment for Mexico specifically (p. 17 discusses it generally); Alfaro and Chor do not measure it.

X-C307.claim: Mexican policymakers and firms show their own agency, not only US-imposed alignment. The government's stated goals (Plan México; the 2025 tariff reform) are import substitution, more national content and regional integration. Mexico and Canada sought USMCA renewal. The steel industry blames China but also opposes US Section 232 tariffs and seeks a regional steel policy. At the same time Mexican and multinational manufacturers keep relying on Chinese inputs (record Q1 2026 imports) and Chinese FDI rose in H1 2026.
X-C307.source_title: Synthesis of X-E904, X-E906, X-E908, X-E912, X-S315, X-S316
X-C307.limitations: Whether Mexico's tariffs are mainly a response to US pressure or to domestic industrial goals is not documented either way (causal link plausible only). The 2026 import and FDI figures are provisional single-source reports.

X-C308.claim: US enforcement has moved from targeting unlawful transshipment (EAPA, origin fraud) towards restricting lawful 'China-linked' content. Examples are the melt-and-pour and smelt-and-cast rules (2024), the White House's broad 'China-linked goods' definition (2026) and rules-of-origin talks in the USMCA review. This blurs the line between mechanism 1 (transshipment) and mechanism 2 (production with Chinese inputs), which researchers keep separate.
X-C308.source_title: Synthesis of X-E902, X-E905, X-E908, X-E910
X-C308.limitations: The outcome of the USMCA rules-of-origin negotiations is unknown as of October 2026.

X-C309.claim: The effects of Mexico's 2024-2026 tariff increases on Chinese imports are not yet established. Early indicators (record Q1 2026 imports from China, record H1 2026 Chinese FDI) suggest limited short-run substitution and possibly 'tariff-jumping' investment, but these are preliminary, single-source and confounded by IMMEX/PROSEC duty-free regimes.
X-C309.source_title: Synthesis of X-S315, X-S316, X-E906, X-E907
X-C309.limitations: Needs INEGI tariff-line data and a 2026 full-year series.

mexico.summary: Documented: Strict transshipment of Chinese goods through Mexico is small in every study we found that tests for it. A Federal Reserve Board decomposition (June 2026) attributes about 53% of the 2014-17 to 2021-24 growth in Mexican exports to the US to diversion from US tariffs on China. Of that growth, about 14% reflects Chinese production in Mexico, about 38% other firms (largely US and other multinationals) and less than 1 point direct transshipment. Banxico finds 'potentially channelled' flows equal to only 0.45% of Mexico's US exports in 2023, as an upper bound. Utar, Cebreros and Torres show IMMEX/GVC firms' US exports rose about 39% by 2021 and that the effect survives netting out Chinese imports. Unlawful evasion exists at case level (CBP EAPA 7801 against Minth Mexico Coatings, 2024). US policy has nonetheless moved toward restricting lawful China-linked content: melt-and-pour (2024), the end of the steel 232 arrangement (March 2025) and the White House 'Great Transshipment Scam' report (August 2026). US leverage has grown through the non-renewal at the USMCA joint review (1 July 2026) and a 10% Section 301 tariff from 24 July 2026 that exempts USMCA goods (88% of imports from Mexico in early 2026). Mexico has acted on its own stated goals of import substitution and national content: tariffs on 544 lines (2024), about 1,463 lines (DOF 29 Dec 2025) and a further decree in April 2026, and Plan México. Contested: Chinese content in Mexican exports, from about 7% (ADB via Dallas Fed) to 'one-third' (Brookings, unsourced). Value-added data agree that Mexican value added is about half and US content about 17-19%. The size of Chinese FDI is also contested: officially about US$710m in 2024 (10th source), while private trackers count US$11.5-14bn cumulative since 2017. Announcements far exceed realisations: BYD is on hold or cancelled, CATL's plans are paused, and Hofusan's US$1bn expansion is announced only. Whether Mexico's tariffs were driven by US pressure is plausible but not documented. Unknown: post-2025 transshipment (most studies cover the 2018-19 episode); the outcome of USMCA rules-of-origin talks; and the effect of the 2026 tariffs. Preliminary reports show record Chinese imports in Q1 2026 (+4.4%) and record Chinese FDI in H1 2026 (US$596m), which would suggest limited substitution and possible tariff-jumping investment.
gaps: Web search budget (shared across agents) was exhausted mid-stream; remaining items were verified only from pages already identified.
OECD TiVA 2025 country note for Mexico: the PDF blocked automated access (robots), so no direct TiVA figures on Chinese value added were verified.
No DOJ criminal or civil case specifically involving transshipment via Mexico was found; DOJ cases found involved other declared origins (for example Repwire, Sept 2024).
Mexican customs (ANAM) enforcement actions against false origin or undervaluation of Chinese goods were not found or verified.
ECLAC's Inversión Extranjera Directa en ALC report and the Secretaría de Economía FDI-by-country dataset were not opened directly; official Chinese FDI figures come via CRS, Dallas Fed and El CEO.
The 2018-2019 Section 301 list dates and rates were not verified on USTR pages (the list page failed to load); no record was created.
Realised investment and employment at Hisense Nuevo León, the Hofusan park's actual tenants and occupancy, and ZC Rubber's plant status are unverified.
The White House OTMP 'Great Transshipment Scam' report was not opened directly; it is described via law-firm and press summaries.
Details of PROSEC changes (2023-2026) and of how IMMEX/PROSEC interact with the 2026 tariffs need checking against DOF texts.
Brookings' 'one-third Chinese value added' figure has no identifiable source; it is recorded as contested.
Ouyang and Shi (LSE, 2024) claim China is the main source of value added in Mexican exports; we could not access the full text to check its method.
Post-2025 product-level evidence on transshipment (after the much higher 2025 US tariffs on China) is scarce.
Mexican government and business statements on China specifically (Sheinbaum, Ebrard, COMCE, AMIA) were only partly covered.

cases.claim: After Secretary Rubio told President Mulino on 2 Feb 2025 that Chinese presence in the canal area was 'unacceptable' and that, absent immediate changes, the US would act under the 1977/1999 treaty, Panama announced it would not renew (and could terminate early) its BRI memorandum and reviewed the Hutchison port concession. Panama's Supreme Court annulled the concession on 29 Jan 2026; from 23–24 Feb 2026 APM Terminals (Maersk) took over Balboa and TiL (MSC) Cristóbal under 18-month interim contracts. Hutchison's US$22.8bn sale to BlackRock–TiL remained stalled in Aug 2026, and Hutchison/PPC are pursuing arbitration.
cases.source_title: Rubio presses Panama to reduce Chinese influence over its canal or face U.S. measures
cases.locator: paragraphs quoting the State Department summary of the Rubio–Mulino meeting
cases.limitations: Interim contracts last 18 months; the final concessionaire is not decided. The COSCO detail rests on anonymous sources.

us_pressure.measure: Diplomatic ultimatum with an implicit treaty-based threat (Rubio visit, 2 Feb 2025), preceded by Trump's 20 Jan 2025 claim that 'we're taking it back'; followed by a security MoU with rotational US presence (9 Apr 2025). No sanction, tariff or legislation specific to the ports.
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: BRI exit: announced directly after the Rubio talks and credited by Rubio to Trump (documented as timing plus US claim; Mulino did not attribute it to pressure). Ports: the transfer came through a Supreme Court constitutional ruling and a Comptroller audit, not an executive act; Hutchison chose to sell for its own commercial reasons; Beijing's SAMR review and reported demand for a COSCO stake stalled the sale.

cases.alternative_offer: No US public financing. The substitute operators are a US-led private consortium (BlackRock–TiL, the stalled sale) and, in practice, European carriers' terminal arms (Maersk's APM Terminals, MSC's TiL) as interim operators.

followups.description: Reuters (via gCaptain): Mulino says Panama's BRI agreement will not be renewed and could be terminated early; Rubio credits '@POTUS leadership'.
APM Terminals begins temporary operation of Balboa and TiL Panama of Cristóbal, each under an 18-month contract, after the annulment of CKHH's concessions.
CK Hutchison says there is 'absolutely nothing to report' on the BlackRock–MSC transaction; PPC seeks damages via arbitration; sources say COSCO is the unnamed additional strategic investor sought.

cases.case: Panama canal ports (CK Hutchison) and Panama's BRI exit, 2025–2026

cases.claim: After Pompeo's October 2018 warning in Panama about Chinese 'predatory' economic activity, the Cortizo government (from July 2019) cooled ties: it dropped the US$4.1bn Chinese-funded Panama–Chiriquí high-speed rail project in September 2019, and the Panama Maritime Authority cancelled the Landbridge-linked Panama Colón Container Port concession in June 2021 for non-payment and delays. US pressure also reportedly ended China's plan for a large embassy at the canal entrance.

us_pressure.measure: Diplomatic warnings (Pompeo in Panama City, Oct 2018); no project-specific sanction or financing condition documented.
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: Colón port: the AMP cited non-payment and development delays; the concession was reinstated, then cancelled again in April 2025 and the land expropriated in Oct 2025 amid a Delaware ownership dispute between Notarc and Landbridge. Rail: Cortizo's fiscal priorities and the project's cost. Metro Line 3 went to Hyundai after the China Railway bid failed technical requirements. Dialogue Chino attributes the shift to US pressure and Cortizo's wish to keep 'distance from China' (historian Aparicio).

cases.alternative_offer: None documented for the rail line or the Colón port. MSC/Notarc later sought to complete the Colón terminal.

followups.description: Executive Decree 90 orders expropriation of 41 PCCP properties on Margarita Island (Colón); the AMP had cancelled the concession in June 2021 and again in April 2025. No US pressure mentioned.

cases.case: Panama: Varela-era China projects (high-speed rail, Colón container port, embassy), 2018–2021

cases.claim: In April 2019 Pompeo warned in Santiago that Huawei was controlled by the Chinese government and that using it posed risks to Chile's citizens. In July 2020 Chile chose the Japanese-proposed route to Australia and New Zealand over the Huawei-backed route ending in Shanghai. The officially stated reason was that all financial indicators favoured that route. Neither trans-Pacific cable was built until the Google–Desarrollo País Humboldt cable (Valparaíso–Sydney) was signed in June 2025; it is approved, with laying planned for late 2026 and commercial operation for 2027.
cases.source_title: En Japón destacan el desaire de Chile a China en la elección de la ruta para el cable transoceánico
cases.locator: body; quote from Subtel's Pamela Gidi
cases.limitations: The 2019 Pompeo remarks concerned Huawei generally (and a 5G proposal in Puerto Williams), not the cable explicitly. The gap of roughly six years between rejecting Huawei and signing a substitute is itself a finding.
cases.quote: todos los indicadores financieros de nuestros estudios señalaban a esta ruta como la más conveniente

us_pressure.measure: Diplomatic statement (Pompeo, Santiago, 12 Apr 2019) warning against Huawei infrastructure and implying limits on US information-sharing; no sanction or financing condition.
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: Subtel said the Australia route was financially the most convenient; Japan lobbied for its own proposal; Chile's interest in landing in Oceania rather than China. Nikkei and El Mostrador frame the choice as Chile being unable to ignore US intentions, but no Chilean official said so.

cases.alternative_offer: Japanese-proposed route (2020, not built); then a US company (Google) with Chilean state participation (Humboldt, 2025).

followups.description: Chile and Google sign the Humboldt cable agreement (14,800 km, Valparaíso–Sydney via French Polynesia; US$300–550m estimated; Chile contributes about US$25m; deployment envisaged for 2027).
Coastal-use commission approves Humboldt; Subtel says laying begins late 2026 and commercial operation is projected for 2027.

cases.case: Chile: Huawei trans-Pacific cable route, 2019–2020, and the Humboldt alternative

cases.claim: In January 2026 Chile's telecom ministry approved, and two days later rescinded, a request linked to China Mobile for a Valparaíso–Hong Kong cable. On 20–21 Feb 2026 the State Department made Transport Minister Juan Carlos Muñoz and two other officials ineligible for US entry, saying they had compromised critical telecommunications infrastructure. Boric said he ordered the retraction after US threats. Under Kast the project is 'in the freezer' with no final decision, and Humboldt has priority.
cases.source_title: U.S. revokes visas for Chilean officials over China undersea cable
cases.limitations: X-E377 (from Wikipedia) said 'scrapped in January 2026'. The verified status is frozen or pending, not formally cancelled, and the visa measure came in February, after the rescission, not before.
cases.quote: generally ineligible for entry into the United States

us_pressure.measure: Concrete measure: visa ineligibility and revocation for a sitting minister and two officials (21 Feb 2026), after US officials summoned Chilean ministry staff to the embassy following the initial approval.
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: The ministry first cited a 'technical error'. The Kast government's ideological alignment with Washington and the availability of Humboldt also explain the freeze. Formally, no final administrative resolution has been adopted (Subtel).

cases.alternative_offer: Humboldt cable (Google with Chilean state firm Desarrollo País), which Kast says he agreed with US representatives to accelerate.

followups.description: Rest of World: Boric said he ordered the retraction after US threats of long-term consequences; after 11 March the US ambassador said the project was 'over'; Kast officials say it 'continues to be assessed'.
Ex-Ante: the file sits with the Defence and Foreign ministries; Kast: 'Primero vamos a concretar el cable Humboldt. Después conversamos'.

cases.case: Chile: China Mobile 'Chile–China Express' cable and US visa revocations, 2026

cases.claim: Brazil endorsed the principles of the US Clean Network on 10 Nov 2020 during Keith Krach's visit, when the US offered financing to Brazilian operators to buy from Western vendors. Yet the 29 Jan 2021 ministerial ordinance allowed Huawei to participate subject to conditions, requiring only a separate private high-security network for federal government communications. After the November 2021 auction, TIM Brasil named Ericsson and Huawei as its 5G equipment suppliers.
cases.source_title: Portaria permite Huawei no leilão do 5G, mas governo exige rede exclusiva
cases.limitations: No evidence was found that the US financing offer was drawn on; this is an absence of evidence, not proof.

us_pressure.measure: Diplomatic campaign (Clean Network joint statement, Nov 2020; Sullivan visit, Aug 2021) plus an unquantified offer of US financing for non-Chinese equipment; no sanction on Brazil.
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: Huawei's installed base in Brazilian 4G networks, the cost of rip-and-replace, operator and agribusiness lobbying, and China's role as Brazil's largest export market. The government-only private network is the only modification, and it is plausibly a concession to US security concerns.

cases.alternative_offer: US financing for operators buying Nokia or Ericsson equipment (amount not disclosed).

followups.description: TIM Brasil names Ericsson and Huawei as 5G equipment suppliers.

cases.claim: Under US pressure from Ambassador Marc Stanley and SOUTHCOM's Gen. Richardson, the Milei government sent an inspection delegation to the Chinese deep-space station in Neuquén (April 2024), but the station kept operating. In 2026 China's request to add equipment was referred to the Defence Ministry, where the Air Force recommended inventories, inspections and no new antenna. In August 2026 Ambassador Lamelas warned that Chinese technology would deter Vaca Muerta investors, and the Neuquén cooperative CALF made public a communication on US visa restrictions for executives expanding Huawei's operations.
cases.source_title: US issues strong warning to Argentina over China: 'It won't help attract investment'
cases.locator: body: Lamelas quotes; CALF paragraph; station paragraph
cases.limitations: The station's operations are unchanged; restriction concerns only expansion, which is still pending. The CALF visa communication is reported second-hand.
cases.quote: And it won't help attract foreign investors to Vaca Muerta.

us_pressure.measure: Diplomatic statements (Stanley, Richardson 2024; Lamelas 2026) and a reported visa-restriction policy applied to executives expanding Huawei (a concrete instrument, but its issuer is not identified in the source).
us_pressure.alternative_explanations: Milei's own alignment with Washington; the station's contract and 2016 civil-use protocol limit Argentine options; the Air Force's recommendations are bureaucratic caution. CALF says it chooses suppliers on technical and economic criteria; it is not known whether it bought from Huawei.

cases.alternative_offer: None for the station. The implied US offer is Vaca Muerta investment conditional on 'trusted' networks.

followups.description: Government delegation (Cosentino, Antelo, ENACOM, CONAE) inspects the station after 'heavy pressure from Washington'; no findings published.
Government evaluates halting the China–Argentina radio telescope (CART) in San Juan and prepares an action plan on the Neuquén base; an official says 'la decisión es reducir la presencia china'.

cases.case: Argentina: Neuquén deep-space station and Huawei network equipment, 2024–2026

cases.claim: Trump's envoy Mauricio Claver-Carone called Argentina's PBoC swap 'extortion' (April 2025), and Treasury Secretary Bessent said Milei was committed to 'getting China out of Argentina' (October 2025), while stating that US aid was not conditioned on ending the swap. Argentina nevertheless renewed the activated US$5bn tranche in April 2025 and, on 5 Aug 2026, the full ~US$19bn line. About US$680m of the activated tranche was outstanding.
cases.source_title: Argentina renews US$19 billion China swap for another five years
cases.limitations: The BA Times body text says the term was 'extended by two years' while the headline says five years.
cases.quote: La asistencia estadounidense no está condicionada al cierre del swap con China.

claims.claim: Across 16 documented cases (2018–2026), the Chinese-linked option was cancelled, transferred, frozen or delayed in 7 (Panama ports/BRI, Panama rail/Colón port, Chile 2019 cable route, Chile 2026 cable, Atucha III, BYD/CATL in Mexico, and partly Neuquén expansion). A source documents US pressure as the cause in only one (Chile 2026: Boric's own statement after US visa revocations). In the rest the link is plausible but shares the outcome with courts (Panama), costs and finance (Atucha, Colón), the Chinese government's own veto (BYD), or route economics (Chile 2020).
claims.limitations: Case selection follows the research brief (salient, documented episodes), so it over-represents visible pressure and under-represents quiet successes or failures. Counts depend on how cases are bundled.

claims.claim: A US or allied alternative was offered in about 9 cases but implemented in only 3–4, and in none was it a like-for-like, US-financed substitute delivered on time: the El Salvador Acajutla LNG plant (operating 2022, not a substitute for the port/SEZ), Panama's interim port operators (European firms Maersk/APM and MSC/TiL, 2026), the Argentina ESF swap (a complement, not a substitute; the PBoC swap was renewed), and Chile's Humboldt cable (partial; signed 2025, operational 2027 at the earliest, six years after Huawei's route was dropped). The DFC Ecuador refinancing, Brazil's 5G vendor financing, the Bolivia MOU and the Meitner SMR were not implemented as of October 2026.

claims.claim: Pressure had no observable effect on large commercially or fiscally attractive projects where no substitute was offered: Chancay (volumes +71% in H1 2026), Brazil's 5G (Huawei retained), Argentina's PBoC swap (renewed 2026), Bogotá Metro Line 1 (>70% built despite the US MDB-financing threat), Guyana's Demerara bridge (opened 2025), the Taiwan switches of 2018 (none reversed), and the utility acquisitions in Peru and Brazil, which drew no specific US objection. claims.claim: The evidence broadly supports 'denial without substitution' in finance and heavy infrastructure, but it qualifies the claim in three ways. (1) Substitution, where it happens, comes mostly from US big tech (Google), allied or European firms (Maersk, MSC, Japan) or private capital (BlackRock, Meitner), not from US public finance. (2) Denial often operates through host-country institutions (Panama's Supreme Court, Chilean ministries, Argentina's NA-SA) or through China's own approval process (BYD), so US pressure is rarely a sufficient cause. (3) Several denials are frozen rather than final (the Chile–China Express file and the Neuquén expansion), and Hutchison's arbitration and the COSCO question keep the Panama outcome open.

The Atucha III annulment (NA-SA meeting, 23 Sep 2026) is single-source (Página/12); NA-SA minutes were not seen.
DFC–Ecuador 2021 framework: the text and telecom-exclusion clause are not public; no evidence of disbursement or formal cancellation was found.
The CALF/Huawei US visa-restriction communication: its sender and legal basis were not identified.
No US objection to State Grid–CPFL (2017) or CSGI–Enel Peru (2024) was found; this is an absence of evidence, not proof.
Bolivia: whether the 2025 Potosí court suspension of the CBC/Uranium One contracts still stands in 2026 was not verified.

Jamaica (Ambassador Tapia's Oct 2020 5G warning about consequences for banking) is documented, but the outcome (which vendors Jamaican operators chose) was not verified, so it was not recorded as a case.

cases.summary: Sixteen episodes of US pressure on Chinese-linked projects or decisions in Latin America (2018–2026) were reconstructed from fetched sources and linked to existing records (PM, X-E) rather than duplicated. The pattern is uneven. Denial outcomes (cancellation, transfer, freeze or delay) occurred in seven cases: Panama's canal ports and BRI exit; the Varela-era rail and Colón port projects; Chile's 2019–20 cable route; Chile's 2026 China Mobile cable; Atucha III (annulled September 2026, single source); BYD and CATL in Mexico; and, partially, expansion of the Neuquén station. Only the 2026 Chile cable has a documented causal link: after US visa revocations against a sitting minister, Boric said he ordered the retraction because of US threats. Elsewhere the outcomes have strong rival explanations: Panama's Supreme Court and audit, unpaid concession fees, Atucha's lack of finance, Chile's stated route economics, and Beijing's own MOFCOM veto on BYD. Pressure had no observable effect in Chancay (H1 2026 volumes +71%), Brazil's 5G (Huawei retained by TIM), Argentina's PBoC swap (fully renewed August 2026 despite Claver-Carone and Bessent), Bogotá Metro Line 1 (>70% built despite US opposition to MDB financing), Guyana's Chinese-built Demerara bridge (opened October 2025), the 2018 Taiwan switches, and the Chinese utility takeovers in Peru and Brazil, where no specific US objection was found. Alternatives were often offered but rarely implemented. The DFC's Ecuador refinancing was not carried out (Ecuador restructured with Chinese banks in 2022). Brazil's 5G financing offer left no trace. Bolivia received only an MOU, and the Atucha substitute (Meitner SMR) is only announced. Implemented substitutes came from European carriers (Maersk, MSC), US big tech (Google's Humboldt, partial until 2027) or a non-equivalent DFC-backed plant (Acajutla LNG). The evidence supports 'denial without substitution' for finance and heavy infrastructure, but qualifies it: denial succeeds mainly in security-coded nodes (ports at the canal, cables, nuclear, space) with already-aligned governments, it works through host institutions and Chinese decisions, and several denials are frozen rather than final. Open questions: the final Panama concessionaire and Hutchison's arbitration; formal NA-SA documentation on Atucha III; whether de la Espriella's Colombia leaves the BRI; and the disbursement record of the DFC Ecuador framework.
